utterance:
Samuel, I've finished examining you, and I want to be straight with you about what I think is going on. Your pain started around the belly button and moved to the lower right side, you've lost your appetite, felt sick and vomited, had a fever, and my examination shows the classic signs of inflammation in that area — it's very tender at a specific point, and it hurts when you cough or move. This picture strongly suggests appendicitis — inflammation of the appendix. That's a common cause of tummy pain in young adults, and it needs urgent treatment in hospital, usually with an operation to remove the appendix. It's not something that will settle on its own, and it's not a stomach bug, unfortunately.

The safest plan is for you to go to the emergency department straight away by ambulance, where they'll do blood tests and a scan, and the surgical team will see you. I'll also give you some pain relief now, and I'd like you to not eat or drink anything from now on, in case you need an operation.

Before I arrange that, can I just double-check — do you take any medications or have any allergies I should know about, including anything over the counter?
reply: An ambulance? Do I really need to make that much of a fuss? Can't my mate just drive me over instead?

utterance:
I understand it feels like a fuss, but yes — I'd really like you to go by ambulance. Here's why: you have a fever and your heart rate is a bit fast, which suggests the inflammation is getting worse, and the pain is now constant and made worse by any movement. If the appendix were to burst on the way, that can make you seriously ill very quickly, and the paramedics can give you pain relief and fluids on the way and pre-warn the hospital so the surgical team is ready. Driving yourself or even being driven by a mate is riskier, and you shouldn't drive with pain this bad. It's much safer this way, and it will get you seen faster.

I'll give you two paracetamol tablets now for the pain, and please don't eat or drink anything else, including water, in case you need an operation today. Are you happy for me to call the ambulance? And can you confirm for me — any allergies to medications, and anything you take regularly, even occasional things like ibuprofen or supplements?
reply: Alright, go ahead and call them. No, I don't take anything regularly and no allergies.

awards.label: Refer to the emergency department today for surgical assessment
Phone the emergency department with a handover

utterance:
The ambulance has been called and I've phoned the emergency department to give them a handover, so they'll know you're coming and why. Here's a summary of what to expect: they'll repeat the examination, take blood tests, and likely do an ultrasound or CT scan of your abdomen to confirm the diagnosis. If it is appendicitis, the usual treatment is an operation to remove the appendix, which is very routine, and you'd stay in hospital for a day or two and be given antibiotics and pain relief.

In the meantime: take the paracetamol I've given you for pain, don't eat or drink anything else, and don't take any ibuprofen or anti-inflammatory tablets. The ambulance should be with you shortly. If anything changes while you wait — for example the pain suddenly gets much worse all over your tummy, you feel faint, you vomit repeatedly, or you feel much hotter — tell the paramedics straight away.

Do you have any questions for me before you go?
reply: An operation? Oh, right. Will I be off work for long?

utterance:
That's a fair question. If it's a straightforward keyhole appendicectomy, most people are back at light duties within about one to two weeks, and back to full physical work — which for an electrician on building sites means no heavy lifting or ladders for around two to four weeks. The hospital team will give you a proper medical certificate and advice tailored to your recovery, so follow what they say. If the appendix has already perforated or there's an infection, recovery can take a bit longer, which is another reason we're getting you treated promptly.

Anything else you'd like to know before the ambulance arrives?

awards.label: Can't-miss diagnosis considered: Perforated viscus with peritonitis
